solution.concept_anchor: Phenological mismatch in Himalayan plant-pollinator networks
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know both A and R are correct but think phenological mismatch is a separate ecological phenomenon unrelated to differential warming rates may choose (b), missing that elevation-dependent warming is the mechanism driving the timing desynchronisation.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Phenological mismatch (earlier flowering vs. delayed pollinator emergence) is an observed and documented consequence of climate change in the Himalayas, disrupting plant-pollinator mutualistic networks.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. The Himalayas experience elevation-dependent warming — higher altitudes warm disproportionately faster, and the overall Himalayan warming rate is 2–3x the global average, confirmed by IPCC AR6.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. Because different elevations warm at different rates, and plants at higher altitudes flower in response to temperature cues while pollinators at lower altitudes emerge on different temperature timelines, differential warming rates directly drive phenological mismatches.
A correct + R correct + R explains A → option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Phenological mismatch is one of the most ecologically consequential climate change impacts in the Himalayas, with cascading effects on pollination-dependent plant reproduction.

Assertion (A): Correct. Earlier spring warming causes alpine plants to flower before their specialist pollinators (bees, butterflies, moths) emerge from dormancy. This temporal desynchronisation reduces pollination success and seed set, threatening plant populations already under climate stress.

Reason (R): Correct. IPCC AR6 and DST reports confirm that the Himalayas are warming 2–3 times faster than the global average. Crucially, this warming is elevation-dependent — higher elevations experience greater temperature increases. This means plants at high altitudes receive stronger warming signals earlier, advancing their phenology more than pollinators at lower elevations.

Causal link: Present. R directly explains A. Differential elevation-dependent warming causes plants and pollinators at different altitudes to receive different temperature-timing cues, creating the mismatch described in A.

Value Addition:
• Similar phenological mismatches are documented in Arctic tundra ecosystems.
• ICIMOD's Hindu Kush Himalaya Assessment (2019) identified phenological shifts as a key early-warning indicator of ecosystem disruption.
• Himalayan bees are particularly vulnerable because their emergence timing is temperature-sensitive and tightly coupled to floral resources.

solution.concept_anchor: Altitudinal sequence of Himalayan forest types
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know conifers are 'higher up' than broadleaf forests but are unsure whether Oak or Rhododendron precedes conifer in the sequence may place broadleaf and conifer in the wrong sub-order, choosing option (b).
elimination_logic: Sub-tropical Sal/Teak forest is the lowest altitudinal zone (up to ~1,000m) — this must be first in the ascending sequence.
Temperate broadleaf Oak-Rhododendron forest follows at 1,000–2,500m — second in the ascending sequence.
Sub-alpine coniferous forest (Deodar, Blue Pine, Silver Fir) occupies 2,500–3,500m — third.
Alpine meadows (bugyals) lie above 3,500m, above the treeline — fourth in ascending sequence, confirming option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) reverses the positions of the Temperate broadleaf and Sub-alpine coniferous zones, placing conifers below oaks. This is a temporal-swap trap that exploits students who have memorised 'conifers' as a Himalayan symbol without anchoring them precisely at 2,500–3,500m versus the oaks at 1,000–2,500m. Students who know both are 'mid-Himalayan forests' without precise altitudinal boundaries will make this reversal.
solution.final_explanation:
The ascending altitudinal sequence of Himalayan forest types corresponds to decreasing temperature and precipitation:

Correct sequence (low to high altitude):
(1) Sub-tropical Sal/Teak → (2) Temperate Oak/Rhododendron → (3) Sub-alpine Coniferous (Deodar, Blue Pine, Fir) → (4) Alpine Meadows (Bugyals)

Why wrong options fail:
• Option placing Conifers before Oaks reverses the 1,000–2,500m vs. 2,500–3,500m sequence.
• Option placing Bugyals before Conifers inverts the treeline logic — bugyals are by definition above the treeline.
• Option placing Sal above Oak would require tropical species to survive at mid-Himalayan altitudes, which is ecologically impossible.

Value Addition:
• This sequence directly mirrors 'latitude-to-altitude' biogeographic principles — ascending the Himalayas from foothills to alpine replicates moving from tropics toward the poles.
• Rhododendron arboreum is the tallest Rhododendron species and is the state tree of Uttarakhand.
• The zone between Sub-alpine and Alpine (roughly 3,500m) is the critical treeline ecotone now shifting upward under climate change.

solution.concept_anchor: Himalayan alpine soils as carbon sinks and India's NDC targets

statement_analysis.statement: Himalayan alpine soils, including those in permafrost-adjacent zones, function as significant carbon sinks and contribute to India's nationally committed target of creating an additional carbon sink of 2.5–3 billion tonnes through forest and tree cover by 2030.
statement_analysis.reason: Alpine soils and Himalayan forests together constitute a significant portion of India's terrestrial carbon storage. India's NDC commits to a 2.5–3 billion tonne additional carbon sink — Himalayan forest states contribute substantially.

statement_analysis.statement: The Payment for Ecosystem Services (PES) mechanism, which compensates communities for protecting forest-based ecosystem services, has been fully and successfully implemented across all Himalayan states in India with standardised payment schedules.
statement_analysis.reason: PES implementation in Himalayan states faces significant challenges including baseline establishment, monitoring difficulties, revenue sharing disputes between states and communities, and lack of standardised frameworks — it has not been 'fully and successfully implemented' with 'standardised payment schedules'.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both PES and India's NDC carbon sink targets are real policy instruments may assume both statements are correct without examining the qualifier 'fully and successfully implemented with standardised payment schedules' in Statement 2.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 correctly links Himalayan alpine soils to carbon storage and India's NDC 2.5–3 billion tonne target — this is factually accurate.

Statement 2's qualifier 'fully and successfully implemented across all Himalayan states with standardised payment schedules' is factually false — PES remains aspirational and faces implementation challenges.
Statement 1 is correct; Statement 2 is incorrect — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a partial-truth trap. PES is a real and discussed policy mechanism in India — students who know 'PES exists and is relevant to Himalayan states' will not question whether implementation has been successful. The trap lies in the qualifier: 'fully and successfully implemented across all Himalayan states with standardised payment schedules' transforms a real-but-aspirational policy into a false claim of achievement. This scope-extension language is the classic UPSC-style trap within PES questions.
solution.final_explanation:
Carbon stocks and ecosystem service valuation mechanisms are critical for Himalayan conservation policy.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Himalayan alpine soils store significant organic carbon, particularly in cool, waterlogged conditions adjacent to permafrost. India's NDC targets an additional 2.5–3 billion tonne carbon sink through forests by 2030, to which Himalayan states (Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh) contribute through their extensive forest cover.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: PES as a concept is applied in parts of Himalayan India (e.g., watershed payments in Himachal Pradesh), but standardised, comprehensive implementation across all Himalayan states with codified payment schedules does not exist. Challenges include defining baselines, attribution of ecosystem services, and equitable benefit sharing with local communities.

Value Addition:
• Himachal Pradesh's 'Green Bonus' demand to the central government is a form of PES argument — requesting compensation for maintaining forests that benefit downstream states.
• India's updated NDC (2022) raises forest carbon sink ambition to 2.5–3 billion tonnes by 2030.
• The Green Climate Fund (GCF) can finance PES-type mechanisms in developing countries through REDD+ results-based payments.

solution.concept_anchor: Transboundary conservation and Snow Leopard range countries

statement_analysis.statement: The Global Snow Leopard and Ecosystem Protection Program (GSLEP) encompasses all 12 range countries of the Snow Leopard and was launched to develop national Snow Leopard conservation plans.
statement_analysis.reason: GSLEP covers all 12 snow leopard range countries (including India, China, Russia, Mongolia, Afghanistan etc.) with the objective of developing national conservation plans — Statement 1 is accurate.

statement_analysis.statement: The Kanchenjunga Landscape conservation initiative connects protected areas in India, Nepal, and China, making it a trilateral transboundary conservation programme.
statement_analysis.reason: The Kanchenjunga Landscape connects protected areas across India, Nepal, and Bhutan — NOT China. Replacing Bhutan with China is a geographic-swap error.

statement_analysis.statement: Hemis National Park in Ladakh is the largest national park in India by area and serves as one of the most important habitats for Snow Leopard in the country.
statement_analysis.reason: Hemis NP (approximately 4,400 sq km) is India's largest national park by area and has one of the highest Snow Leopard densities globally — Statement 3 is accurate.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who doubt the GSLEP country count (12) but are confident about Hemis may select option (c) (only Statement 1 incorrect), when in fact Statement 2 is the one with the error.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: GSLEP covers 12 range countries — factually accurate; NOT a wrong statement.
Statement 2: Kanchenjunga Landscape links India-Nepal-Bhutan, not India-Nepal-China — the inclusion of China is a geographic-swap making this statement wrong.
Statement 3: Hemis NP is India's largest NP and a key snow leopard habitat — factually accurate; NOT a wrong statement.
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The China-Bhutan swap in Statement 2 exploits the geographic proximity of China to both Kanchenjunga and the Snow Leopard range. Students who know China is a major snow leopard range country may unconsciously accept 'China' as a Kanchenjunga Landscape partner. But the Kanchenjunga Landscape is specifically an India-Nepal-Bhutan initiative, as all three countries share the Kanchenjunga mountain massif and its associated biodiversity corridors — China does not border this landscape.
solution.final_explanation:
Transboundary conservation in the Himalayas reflects the reality that biodiversity ignores political boundaries.

• Statement 1 — Correct: GSLEP (launched 2013 in Bishkek) brings together all 12 snow leopard range countries — Afghanistan, Bhutan, China, India, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Myanmar, Nepal, Pakistan, Russia, and Tajikistan — around a shared conservation framework.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Kanchenjunga Landscape is a trilateral conservation initiative connecting protected areas in India (Sikkim, West Bengal), Nepal (Kangchenjunga Conservation Area), and Bhutan (Jigme Dorji NP network) — not China. China does not share the Kanchenjunga massif.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Hemis NP at ~4,400 sq km is India's largest national park. Its high-altitude rocky terrain in Ladakh supports one of the world's densest snow leopard populations.

Value Addition:
• The Kanchenjunga Landscape supports tigers, snow leopards, and red pandas across the three nations.
• India's Project Snow Leopard (2009) focuses on 5 Himalayan states: J&K (now UT), Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, and Arunachal Pradesh.
• Snow leopard was downlisted from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2017 — reflecting population recovery through conservation.

solution.concept_anchor: ICIMOD Hindu Kush Himalaya Assessment 2019 findings
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who associate climate change reports with IPCC and know IPCC AR6 references Himalayan vulnerability may select option (b), not distinguishing between the IPCC's global report and ICIMOD's region-specific assessment.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): The '2°C scenario projecting one-third glacier loss by 2100' is from ICIMOD's Hindu Kush Himalaya Assessment 2019 — attributing it to IPCC SR1.5 is incorrect.
Eliminate option (b): IPCC AR6 (2021) addresses Himalayan warming but the specific 'one-third glacier loss' projection at 2°C comes from ICIMOD's dedicated regional assessment, not AR6.
Eliminate option (d): The Chamoli 2021 event is linked to a rock-ice avalanche and GLOF cascade, not to the ICIMOD assessment report itself — the pairing conflates two unrelated items.
Option (c) correctly pairs the Hindu Kush Himalaya Assessment (2019) by ICIMOD with the finding that one-third of Himalayan glaciers could be lost by 2100 even under a 2°C warming scenario.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap operates by attributing the ICIMOD 2019 finding to the IPCC SR1.5 or AR6 — documents students are more likely to have studied. ICIMOD's Hindu Kush Himalaya Assessment is a standalone regional scientific assessment, not an IPCC report, but it was published around the same time as IPCC SR1.5 (2018) and covers similar climate scenarios. Students who know 'a major 2018–2019 climate report projected Himalayan glacier loss' but misremember the authoring body will select option (a) or (b).
solution.final_explanation:
Scientific assessments on Himalayan cryosphere vulnerability are crucial for UPSC policy questions.

• Option (a): Incorrect. IPCC Special Report on 1.5°C (SR1.5, 2018) covers global implications of warming levels but does not contain the specific 'one-third Himalayan glacier loss' regional projection. Wrong attribution.
• Option (b): Incorrect. IPCC AR6 (2021) discusses Himalayan warming rates and cryosphere loss in a global context but the regional-specific 'one-third glacier' figure comes from ICIMOD, not AR6.
• Option (c): Correct. The Hindu Kush Himalaya Assessment (2019), produced by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), specifically projects that one-third of the Hindu Kush Himalayan glaciers will be lost by 2100 even if global warming is limited to 2°C — a landmark finding for Himalayan policy.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Chamoli 2021 is a disaster event linked to a GLOF/rock-ice avalanche — not a finding of the ICIMOD Assessment report.

Value Addition:
• ICIMOD is headquartered in Kathmandu, Nepal.
• The HKH Assessment covered 8 countries: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, China, India, Myanmar, Nepal, and Pakistan.
• Under a 1.5°C scenario, only about 36% of glaciers would be lost — demonstrating the critical difference ambition makes.

solution.concept_anchor: Pangong Tso Ramsar status and Central Asian Flyway

statement_analysis.statement: Pangong Tso in Ladakh, despite being the most celebrated high-altitude lake in India, is not designated as a Ramsar Wetland of International Importance.
statement_analysis.reason: Pangong Tso is not a Ramsar site. Tsomoriri in Ladakh holds the Ramsar designation — this is a frequently tested distinction.

statement_analysis.statement: The Central Asian Flyway passes over the Himalayan region, and high-altitude wetlands like Tsomoriri serve as critical breeding and staging grounds for migratory waterfowl including the Bar-headed goose.
statement_analysis.reason: The Central Asian Flyway covers migration routes passing over the Himalayas. Tsomoriri and similar Trans-Himalayan wetlands are breeding sites for Bar-headed goose and staging areas for the Black-necked crane.

statement_analysis.statement: The Black-necked crane, which breeds in high-altitude Trans-Himalayan wetlands, is the state bird of Sikkim and is also listed under Schedule I of the Wildlife Protection Act 1972.
statement_analysis.reason: The state bird of Sikkim is the Blood Pheasant (Ithaginis cruentus), not the Black-necked crane. The Black-necked crane is significant in Sikkim culturally but is not its state bird. (Black-necked crane is state bird of Arunachal Pradesh in some classifications — but not Sikkim.)

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know Black-necked crane is culturally significant in Sikkim (it features in Sikkimese festivals) may assume it is also the state bird, leading them to mark all three statements correct and select option (c).
elimination_logic: Statement 1 correctly distinguishes Pangong Tso (not Ramsar) from Tsomoriri (Ramsar) — Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2 correctly describes the Central Asian Flyway and Tsomoriri's role for migratory birds — Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 3 erroneously identifies the Black-necked crane as Sikkim's state bird — the state bird of Sikkim is the Blood Pheasant; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Only Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Black-necked crane is deeply associated with Sikkim through the Tsechu festival and is culturally revered — this cultural prominence causes students to attribute state bird status to it. The entity-swap substitutes the Blood Pheasant (actual state bird) with the Black-necked crane (culturally prominent but not the state symbol). This tests whether students separate ecological/cultural significance from official government designations.
solution.final_explanation:
High-altitude Himalayan wetlands serve as critical nodes in the Central Asian Flyway and support iconic avifauna.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Pangong Tso, despite its global fame, is not a Ramsar site. Tsomoriri (Ladakh) is the Ramsar-designated wetland in the Trans-Himalayan zone.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Central Asian Flyway is one of nine global flyways and passes over the Himalayas. Trans-Himalayan wetlands like Tsomoriri serve as breeding grounds for Bar-headed goose and staging areas for other migratory waterfowl.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The state bird of Sikkim is the Blood Pheasant (Ithaginis cruentus), not the Black-necked crane. The crane is culturally important in Sikkim (featured in Tsechu festivals) but does not hold the official state bird designation.

Value Addition:
• Black-necked crane is designated as the state bird of Arunachal Pradesh.
• Bar-headed goose holds the world record for highest-altitude bird migration, crossing the Himalayas at over 7,000m.
• Tsomoriri is also a proposed UNESCO biosphere reserve due to its ecological and cultural significance.

solution.concept_anchor: Joshimath subsidence and Zone V geological fragility
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know Joshimath is associated with the Char Dham pilgrimage route and hydropower construction may attribute the subsidence to a single cause (dam construction vibration) rather than the combination of geological fragility, seismicity, and construction pressure.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a hill town on steep slopes with immature soils experiencing land subsidence after rapid construction — this matches the Joshimath profile.
Eliminate option (b): 'Volcanic soil compaction' is a plausible-fabrication — the Himalayas are NOT volcanic; they are fold mountains formed by tectonic collision, with no volcanic activity.

Eliminate option (c): Hydropower dam vibration as the sole cause is an oversimplification; the geological fragility arises from multiple factors including immature soils, seismic Zone V, and slope instability.
Eliminate option (d): Anthropogenic river damming upstream is irrelevant to land subsidence on hill slopes — flooding would be a different mechanism.

Option (a) correctly identifies the combination of immature Himalayan soils (Inceptisols/Entisols), seismic Zone V activity, and concentrated construction loading as the multi-causal explanation for the subsidence.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) introduces 'volcanic soil compaction' — a plausible-fabrication that sounds geologically credible to a student who associates 'soil compaction' with construction damage. Himalayan soils are not volcanic (unlike Deccan basalt soils); they are young, alluvial or colluvial deposits from ongoing erosion. The mention of 'volcanic' is the planted fabrication. Students who read quickly may accept the compaction mechanism without questioning the volcanic origin.
solution.final_explanation:
The Joshimath subsidence crisis (2023) exemplifies the intersection of geological fragility, seismicity, and development pressure in the Himalayas.

Applying the principle: The scenario describes a hill town on steep slopes with immature soils, in a seismically active zone, experiencing subsidence from rapid construction — this multi-causal explanation is the correct framework.

• Option (a): Correct. Himalayan slopes bear immature Inceptisols and Entisols with poor load-bearing capacity. Joshimath falls in Seismic Zone V (highest risk). Rapid, unregulated construction concentrated loads on geologically fragile slopes — triggering progressive failure. This multi-causal analysis correctly applies Himalayan geological principles.
• Option (b): Incorrect. 'Volcanic soil compaction' is a fabricated mechanism. The Himalayas have no volcanic activity — they are fold mountains from plate collision. Himalayan soils are erosional deposits, not volcanic.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Hydropower dam vibration is one contributing stressor but not the primary geological explanation. The scenario requires identifying foundational geological fragility, not a single construction activity.
• Option (d): Incorrect. River damming upstream causes reservoir-related issues — not slope subsidence at higher elevations above the river.

Value Addition:
• Joshimath/Auli is in the Chamoli district of Uttarakhand, on the path to Badrinath.
• The town sits on an ancient landslide deposit — building on such material carries inherent instability risk.
• National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) has flagged over 60 Himalayan towns with similar subsidence risk profiles.

Which of the following most accurately explains the primary geophysical mechanism driving this crisis?

(b) Volcanic soil compaction beneath the town, triggered by residual magmatic activity in the deeper Himalayan crust, causing the soil matrix to collapse under building weight
(c) Vibrations from a nearby hydropower dam's tunnel blasting operations, which are the sole cause of the soil failure and structural damage to buildings
(d) Upstream river damming reducing sediment supply to the valley floor, causing downstream slope undercutting and gradual upslope retrogressive failure

solution.concept_anchor: Sangai and Himalayan Quail as Himalayan endemic species
solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who associate 'Himalayan endemic bird' with the Himalayan Quail may select it, but the question specifies a critically rare animal connected to the Eastern Himalayan foothills wetlands, pointing away from a bird species.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Mishmi takin is endemic to Arunachal Pradesh (Eastern Himalayas) but is a bovid — not the specific species tested here.
Eliminate option (c): Himalayan Quail (Ophrysia superciliosa) is possibly extinct — last confirmed sighting in 1876 — and is a bird, not a mammal of wetland origin.
Eliminate option (d): Chiru (Tibetan antelope) is a Trans-Himalayan cold desert species, not an Eastern Himalayan foothills wetland species.

Option (b) Manipur brow-antlered deer (Sangai, Rucervus eldii eldii) is the correct answer — it is an Endangered endemic cervid of the floating meadows (Phumdi) of Loktak Lake, Manipur — in the Eastern Himalayan fringe.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Sangai is one of India's rarest endemic mammals, but students may confuse it with the Chiru (also horned), or with Mishmi takin (also Northeast India). The entity-swap here involves knowing that 'brow-antlered' refers specifically to the Sangai's unique antler shape, and that its habitat is the floating phumdi islands of Loktak Lake — a very specific ecology at the Eastern Himalayan fringe, not the high-altitude zones where other listed options reside.
solution.final_explanation:
The Eastern Himalayas and their fringe support some of India's most exclusive endemic species.

• Option (a) Mishmi takin: A bovid endemic to the Mishmi Hills of Arunachal Pradesh. Ecologically valid for Eastern Himalayas but not the species associated with floating-meadow wetlands.
• Option (b) Sangai (Manipur brow-antlered deer, Rucervus eldii eldii): Correct. Found exclusively on the floating phumdi islands of Loktak Lake, Manipur — the only population of this subspecies. It is Endangered and the state animal of Manipur.
• Option (c) Himalayan Quail: A bird, possibly extinct (last seen 1876), associated with grassy hill slopes — not a wetland cervid.
• Option (d) Chiru (Tibetan antelope): A Trans-Himalayan cold desert species living above 4,000m — completely different ecological zone.

Value Addition:
• Sangai is the state animal of Manipur and is listed under Schedule I of WPA 1972.
• Keibul Lamjao National Park in Loktak Lake is the world's only floating national park.
• Loktak Lake is a Ramsar site and the largest freshwater lake in Northeast India.

statement_analysis.statement: The 'plus' in REDD+ extends the framework beyond reducing deforestation to include sustainable forest management, conservation of existing carbon stocks, and enhancement of forest carbon stocks through activities such as afforestation.
statement_analysis.reason: REDD+ explicitly includes a 'plus' component covering sustainable forest management, conservation, and enhancement of carbon stocks — including afforestation and reforestation — going beyond the core REDD deforestation and degradation reduction.

statement_analysis.statement: India's Nationally Determined Contribution commits to creating an additional carbon sink of 2.5–3 billion tonnes of CO₂ equivalent through forests and tree cover by 2030.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the precise NDC target — 2.5–3 billion tonnes of CO₂ equivalent additional carbon sink through forest and tree cover by 2030, maintained in India's updated 2022 NDC.

statement_analysis.statement: Under REDD+, countries receive results-based payments only after demonstrating avoided deforestation; no payments are possible for activities related to sustainable forest management or forest carbon stock enhancement.
statement_analysis.reason: Results-based REDD+ payments can be received for all five REDD+ activities, including sustainable forest management and carbon stock enhancement — not only for avoided deforestation. Statement 3 wrongly restricts eligibility to one activity.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know REDD+ is primarily about deforestation may assume Statement 3 is correct (payments only for avoided deforestation), accepting all three as true and selecting option (d).
elimination_logic: Statement 1 correctly describes the 'plus' components of REDD+ — it is accurate.
Statement 2 correctly states India's NDC forest carbon sink target — 2.5–3 billion tonnes CO₂ equivalent by 2030.
Statement 3 incorrectly restricts REDD+ results-based payments to avoided deforestation only — all five REDD+ activities are eligible for results-based payments.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct; Statement 3 is not — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses scope-extension by adding 'only' to a claim about REDD+ payment eligibility. Students who know deforestation is REDD's core focus may not scrutinise whether sustainable forest management and carbon stock enhancement also qualify for results-based payments under the 'plus' framework. The word 'only' transforms a partial truth (deforestation is the core focus) into a false absolute.
solution.final_explanation:
The REDD+ framework has five defined activity types, each eligible for results-based finance.

• Statement 1 — Correct: REDD+ 'plus' components extend beyond deforestation reduction to include: (i) sustainable forest management, (ii) conservation of forest carbon stocks, and (iii) enhancement of forest carbon stocks (afforestation, reforestation). All five activities together constitute REDD+.
• Statement 2 — Correct: India's NDC forest carbon sink target — 2.5–3 billion tonnes CO₂ equivalent by 2030 — is a firm national commitment, maintained and reaffirmed in the updated 2022 NDC submission.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Results-based REDD+ payments under the UNFCCC and through vehicles like the Green Climate Fund are available for all five REDD+ activities — including sustainable forest management and carbon stock enhancement, not solely avoided deforestation.

Value Addition:
• The five REDD+ activities are: (1) Reducing deforestation, (2) Reducing forest degradation, (3) Conservation of carbon stocks, (4) Sustainable management of forests, (5) Enhancement of carbon stocks.
• Green Climate Fund (GCF) and Forest Carbon Partnership Facility (FCPF) are key REDD+ financing vehicles.
• India submitted its updated NDC in August 2022, maintaining the 2.5–3 billion tonne forest carbon sink target.
